title: Pleural infection and empyema (adult)
subject: respiratory
summary: Aspirate any effusion with suspected infection under ultrasound and measure pH immediately: frank pus or pH 7.2 or less needs a small-bore chest drain; pH above 7.2 to below 7.4 needs LDH and clinical review. Give antibiotics with anaerobic cover for 2 to 6 weeks, tPA plus DNase for residual collections, and refer early for VATS when medical treatment fails.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Suspect pleural infection in pneumonia with an effusion, or persisting fever and raised CRP despite antibiotics; also after thoracic surgery, trauma, oesophageal rupture or aspiration.
Pleural infection includes complicated parapneumonic effusion (CPPE) and empyema (frank pus). Up to 20% of patients die within 12 months and about 15% need surgery.

RAPID score (BTS 2023): Renal (urea below 5 mmol/L 0, 5 to 8 mmol/L 1, above 8 mmol/L 2), Age (below 50 0, 50 to 70 1, above 70 2), Purulence (purulent 0, non-purulent 1), Infection source (community 0, hospital 1), Diet (albumin above 27 g/L 0, below 27 g/L 1). 0 to 2 low, 3 to 4 medium, 5 to 7 high risk.
Common organisms: S. pneumoniae, S. aureus, streptococci (including S. anginosus group), anaerobes and, in India, Klebsiella and other Gram-negatives. Consider TB in a lymphocytic exudate.

sections.title: Pleural aspiration and tests
items: Always use thoracic ultrasound guidance for aspiration. Send fluid in a plain container and inoculate 5 to 10 mL into aerobic and anaerobic blood culture bottles.
Measure pleural pH immediately in a blood gas analyser (no heparin or local anaesthetic contamination, no air in the syringe, no delay) unless the fluid is frank pus.
Also send glucose, LDH, protein (with serum protein and LDH for Light's criteria), cell count, Gram stain and culture; in India add AFB smear, TB NAAT and ADA.
Blood cultures, CBC, CRP, urea, creatinine, albumin, glucose. Contrast CT thorax if the diagnosis or drain position is unclear or the patient is not improving.
If immediate pH is unavailable, pleural glucose below 60 mg/dL (3.3 mmol/L) indicates a high probability of CPPE or pleural infection.

sections.title: Drainage decision (BTS 2023)
items: Frank pus, or pH 7.2 or less: high risk; insert an intercostal drain if ultrasound shows a safe accessible pocket.

pH above 7.2 and below 7.4: intermediate risk; measure LDH and consider a drain if LDH is above 900 IU/L, especially with a large effusion, pleural glucose 72 mg/dL (4.0 mmol/L) or less, pleural contrast enhancement on CT, septations on ultrasound, or ongoing fever.
pH 7.4 or more: low risk; no immediate drain, but review regularly and re-aspirate if not improving. Septated effusions with pH above 7.4 should also be considered for drainage.
Use a small-bore chest tube (14F or smaller; 12 to 14F in the treatment pathway). Early VATS or medical thoracoscopy is not recommended as the initial treatment.
Remember mimics of a low-pH effusion: rheumatoid effusion, advanced malignancy or mesothelioma, oesophageal rupture.

sections.title: Antibiotics and supportive care
items: Start antibiotics before culture results, always covering anaerobes. Community-acquired example: cefuroxime (or ceftriaxone) plus metronidazole, or IV amoxicillin-clavulanate. Hospital-acquired: cover resistant Gram-negatives and possibly MRSA, e.g. meropenem plus vancomycin. Follow the local antibiogram.
Narrow therapy once cultures return; pneumococcal infection is usually monomicrobial.
Duration is usually 2 to 6 weeks guided by clinical response: IV in hospital, then oral (e.g. amoxicillin-clavulanate) once inflammatory markers fall significantly.
Give VTE prophylaxis and assess nutrition (low albumin predicts poor outcome). Confirmed TB empyema: drain and start anti-TB treatment.

sections.title: Intrapleural therapy and surgery
items: Residual collection after drainage has stopped: intrapleural tPA 10 mg plus DNase 5 mg twice daily for 3 days (6 doses). A lower tPA dose (5 mg twice daily with DNase 5 mg) may be as effective and suits patients with higher bleeding risk. Obtain consent for bleeding risk.
Do not use single-agent tPA or DNase, or streptokinase. Saline irrigation is an option when tPA plus DNase and surgery are unsuitable.
Refer directly for surgery (VATS preferred over thoracotomy) if the patient is clinically unstable or imaging shows profound pleural thickening or a solid collection.

Poor progress (persistent pleural shadowing with static or rising inflammatory markers): CT, then intrapleural therapy or surgery. Use intrapleural therapy if surgery will be delayed by more than 48 hours.
Not fit for surgery: change or prolong antibiotics, consider non-intubated surgical options such as rib resection, or an indwelling pleural catheter.

sections.title: Monitoring
items: Daily review of temperature, drain output and position, CRP and WBC; repeat ultrasound or chest X-ray to confirm the collection is resolving.
Remove the drain when there is little residual pleural shadowing and the patient is improving.
Arrange CT follow-up for ongoing symptoms or other concerning features to exclude occult malignancy.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Delaying drainage of pus or a pH 7.2 or less effusion while trying antibiotics alone.
pH measured by a urine dipstick or pH paper, or on a heparinised or air-contaminated sample.
Omitting anaerobic cover, or stopping antibiotics after 5 to 7 days as for simple pneumonia.
Late surgical referral when medical therapy is failing; missing TB, malignancy or an oesophageal leak (fungal pleural infection should prompt a search for one).

drugs.name: Tissue plasminogen activator (alteplase), intrapleural
drugs.dose: 10 mg via chest drain twice daily for 3 days (6 doses); 5 mg twice daily if higher bleeding risk
drugs.notes: Always combined with DNase; follow BTS Clinical Statement on Pleural Procedures for administration.

drugs.name: Dornase alfa (DNase), intrapleural
drugs.dose: 5 mg via chest drain twice daily for 3 days (6 doses)
drugs.notes: Given with tPA; not as single agent.

drugs.name: Amoxicillin-clavulanate
drugs.dose: 1.2 g IV every 8 hours; oral step-down 625 mg three times daily
drugs.notes: Covers streptococci and anaerobes; reduce dose if eGFR below 30 mL/min.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone plus metronidazole
drugs.dose: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily plus metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours

drugs.name: Meropenem
drugs.notes: Hospital-acquired infection; add vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV every 12 hours (adjusted to levels) if MRSA risk.
